questions.stem: A firewall log shows administrators connecting to switches on TCP 23. Which two statements about the protocol on that port are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: It provides remote command-line access
options.rationale: Correct: TCP 23 is Telnet.

options.text: It sends everything, including passwords, in cleartext
options.rationale: Correct: Telnet has no encryption.

options.text: It encrypts sessions with keys exchanged at login
options.rationale: That describes SSH on TCP 22.

options.text: It is used to transfer configuration files over UDP
options.rationale: That describes TFTP on UDP 69.

options.text: It synchronizes device clocks
options.rationale: That is NTP on UDP 123.

questions.explanation: Telnet provides remote command-line access over TCP 23. It is cleartext, so credentials are exposed; SSH on TCP 22 is the secure replacement.
questions.discriminator_tested: Telnet: TCP 23, cleartext.

questions.stem: An analyst who once recovered a password from a Telnet capture tries the same on the session below. What will they MOST likely find?
questions.exhibit:
10.1.9.40:50112 > 10.1.1.2:22   SSH  Client: Protocol (SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6)
10.1.1.2:22 > 10.1.9.40:50112   SSH  Server: Protocol (SSH-2.0-Cisco-1.25)
10.1.9.40:50112 > 10.1.1.2:22   SSH  Client: Key Exchange Init
10.1.1.2:22 > 10.1.9.40:50112   SSH  Server: Key Exchange Init
10.1.9.40:50112 > 10.1.1.2:22   SSH  Client: Encrypted packet (len=96)

options.text: Only encrypted packets after the key exchange
options.rationale: Correct: the login happens inside the encrypted channel.

options.text: The SSH versions of the client and server
options.rationale: Visible, but useless for recovering the password.

options.text: The password in cleartext, as with Telnet
options.rationale: SSH encrypts the login.

options.text: The password in the Key Exchange Init packet
options.rationale: Key exchange happens before the login and carries no password.

questions.explanation: SSH provides encrypted remote access over TCP 22. Keys are negotiated first, and everything after that, including the login, is encrypted; it is the secure replacement for Telnet.
questions.discriminator_tested: SSH is encrypted; the secure replacement for Telnet.

questions.stem: A nightly job uploads payroll files to a partner over FTP. Which replacement BEST protects both the login and the files?

options.text: SFTP, running the transfer inside SSH
options.rationale: Correct: credentials and data are both encrypted.

options.text: Zip the files with a password before using FTP
options.rationale: Protects the file contents, but the FTP login is still cleartext.

options.text: TFTP, which has less overhead
options.rationale: TFTP has no authentication or encryption at all.

options.text: FTP with a longer, stronger password
options.rationale: A strong password still crosses the network in cleartext.

questions.explanation: FTP transfers files over TCP 20/21 with credentials and data in cleartext. SFTP, tunneled through SSH, encrypts both.
questions.discriminator_tested: FTP: credentials and data in cleartext.

questions.stem: Which two statements about SFTP are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: It runs over SSH on TCP port 22
options.rationale: Correct: it is file transfer inside SSH.

options.text: It encrypts both credentials and file data
options.rationale: Correct: everything travels inside the SSH tunnel.

options.text: It is FTP with a stronger password policy
options.rationale: It is a different protocol, not hardened FTP.

options.text: It uses UDP 69 with no authentication
options.rationale: That describes TFTP.

options.text: It is the same protocol as FTPS
options.rationale: FTPS adds TLS to FTP; SFTP runs over SSH.

questions.explanation: SFTP is file transfer tunneled through SSH (TCP 22): encrypted, and not the same as FTP or TFTP.
questions.discriminator_tested: SFTP is encrypted and runs over SSH.

questions.stem: Switches pull their configuration files from a TFTP server each time they boot. What is the MAIN security weakness of this design?

options.text: No login is needed to fetch configs
options.rationale: Correct: TFTP has no authentication, so anyone who can reach it can pull configs.

options.text: Transfers may fail because UDP is unreliable
options.rationale: TFTP handles its own acknowledgments; this is a reliability point, not security.

options.text: The server must hold an SSH key for each switch
options.rationale: TFTP doesn't use SSH.

options.text: TFTP sends configs to the internet by default
options.rationale: It sends files only to whoever requests them.

questions.explanation: TFTP is simple file transfer over UDP 69 with no authentication, used for configuration, firmware, and boot files. Anyone who can reach the server can request a config, passwords and all.
questions.discriminator_tested: TFTP has no authentication.

questions.stem: A firewall must let a monitoring server poll switches and also receive the alerts the switches send. Which rules does it need?

options.text: UDP 161 to the switches, UDP 162 back to the server
options.rationale: Correct: polling goes to 161; traps come back to 162.

options.text: TCP 161 to the switches, TCP 162 back to the server
options.rationale: SNMP uses UDP.

options.text: UDP 162 to the switches, UDP 161 back to the server
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: TCP 22 both ways, since SNMP runs over SSH
options.rationale: SNMP doesn't run over SSH.

questions.explanation: SNMP monitors and manages network devices over UDP 161, with traps on UDP 162.
questions.discriminator_tested: SNMP: UDP 161 for polling; traps on 162.

questions.stem: A public website still serves its login page and member pages over HTTP. Which change BEST fixes this?

options.text: Serve the site over HTTPS and redirect HTTP to it
options.rationale: Correct: every page, and the session, is encrypted.

options.text: Move just the login page to HTTPS, keeping the rest on HTTP
options.rationale: Protects the password, but session cookies still travel in cleartext.

options.text: Serve the site on port 8080 instead of 80
options.rationale: A different port is still cleartext HTTP.

options.text: Add a login CAPTCHA to stop automated attacks
options.rationale: Doesn't encrypt anything.

questions.explanation: HTTP carries web traffic over TCP 80 in cleartext. Serving the whole site over HTTPS (TLS on 443) and redirecting HTTP protects logins and sessions alike.
questions.discriminator_tested: HTTP is cleartext.

questions.stem: A user sees the warning below when opening the company portal. What does it MOST likely mean?
questions.exhibit:
https://portal.example.com
Your connection is not private
NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID
Certificate: issued to *.example.net   issued by Example Issuing CA

options.text: The certificate is for a different name
options.rationale: Correct: the certificate is for *.example.net, not portal.example.com.

options.text: The connection may not be secure
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say why the browser objected.

options.text: The page is using HTTP instead of HTTPS
options.rationale: The address is HTTPS; the problem is the certificate.

options.text: The user's password has expired
options.rationale: Certificate errors have nothing to do with the user's password.

questions.explanation: HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS over TCP 443: encrypted and authenticated. The certificate authenticates the server, so a name mismatch means the browser can't confirm it is talking to the real portal, which may indicate interception.
questions.discriminator_tested: HTTPS is authenticated: the certificate must match the server.

questions.stem: Logs from 40 devices must line up to the second for incident investigations. Which protocol and port should each device be configured to use?

options.text: NTP on UDP 123
options.rationale: Correct: clock synchronization.

options.text: SNMP on UDP 161
options.rationale: SNMP manages devices; it doesn't set their clocks.

options.text: DNS on UDP 53
options.rationale: DNS resolves names.

options.text: NTP on TCP 23
options.rationale: Right protocol, wrong port: TCP 23 is Telnet.

questions.explanation: NTP synchronizes clocks over UDP 123. Consistent time matters for logs and certificates.
questions.discriminator_tested: NTP: UDP 123; consistent time for logs.

questions.stem: What BEST explains why DNS sometimes uses TCP instead of UDP?

options.text: For large responses and zone transfers
options.rationale: Correct: these exceed what a single UDP reply handles well.

options.text: Because TCP is more reliable
options.rationale: True of TCP, but not the specific trigger for DNS.

options.text: Because queries to external servers require it
options.rationale: Ordinary external queries use UDP.

options.text: To encrypt queries between resolvers
options.rationale: Plain TCP doesn't encrypt anything.

questions.explanation: DNS resolves names to IP addresses on port 53, using UDP for normal queries and TCP for large responses and zone transfers.
questions.discriminator_tested: DNS: UDP for queries; TCP for large responses and zone transfers.

questions.stem: After a new switch is installed, PCs in one area start getting 169.254.x.x addresses, while PCs elsewhere are fine. The DHCP server is up. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: DHCP requests from that area aren't reaching the server
options.rationale: Correct: the new switch's path or relay is blocking them, so the PCs fall back to APIPA.

options.text: The new switch is blocking those PCs' traffic
options.rationale: Possibly, but too general: the DHCP exchange specifically is failing.

options.text: The PCs are configured with static addresses
options.rationale: Static addresses wouldn't change to 169.254.

options.text: The DHCP server gave them APIPA addresses
options.rationale: APIPA is self-assigned when no server answers.

questions.explanation: DHCP automatically assigns IP configuration over UDP 67 and 68. A 169.254 address is the symptom; the cause is that the DHCP exchange never completes from that part of the network.
questions.discriminator_tested: DHCP failure shows up as APIPA addresses.

questions.stem: An old print server is set up so that, at boot, a server hands it a fixed IP address based on its MAC address, and that mapping never changes. Which protocol BEST describes this design?

options.text: BootP
options.rationale: Correct: a static MAC-to-IP mapping is BootP's model.

options.text: DHCP
options.rationale: DHCP can reserve addresses, but its defining feature is dynamic assignment.

options.text: APIPA
options.rationale: APIPA is self-assigned, not handed out by a server.

options.text: ARP
options.rationale: ARP maps IPs to MACs on demand; it doesn't assign addresses.

questions.explanation: BootP is the older predecessor of DHCP, using UDP 67/68 with a static MAC-to-IP mapping. DHCP adds dynamic assignment.
questions.discriminator_tested: BootP = static MAC-to-IP mapping.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes an APIPA address from an RFC 1918 private address?

options.text: It's self-assigned and link-local
options.rationale: Correct: no server assigns it, and it can't be routed.

options.text: It starts with 169.254 instead of 10 or 192.168
options.rationale: True, but that is the range, not what it means.

options.text: It is routable on the internet without NAT
options.rationale: APIPA addresses aren't routable at all.

options.text: It is assigned by the DHCP server as a fallback
options.rationale: It appears precisely because no DHCP server answered.

questions.explanation: APIPA self-assigns a 169.254.0.0/16 address when no DHCP server answers. It signals a DHCP failure and is link-local only, with no gateway.
questions.discriminator_tested: APIPA is self-assigned and link-local only.

questions.stem: Which two features does TCP provide that UDP does not? (Choose two.)

options.text: Acknowledgments and retransmission
options.rationale: Correct: TCP confirms delivery and resends losses.

options.text: Sequencing so data arrives in order
options.rationale: Correct: TCP reorders segments.

options.text: Port numbers to identify the service
options.rationale: Both TCP and UDP use ports.

options.text: Low overhead for real-time traffic
options.rationale: That is UDP's strength.

options.text: Encryption of the payload
options.rationale: Neither encrypts; that is TLS's job.

questions.explanation: TCP is connection-oriented, reliable delivery with a three-way handshake, sequencing, and acknowledgments. UDP is connectionless and best-effort.
questions.discriminator_tested: TCP provides reliability and ordering.

questions.stem: DNS queries, DHCP, TFTP, and SNMP all share one transport protocol. Which is it, and which reason BEST explains why it suits them?

options.text: UDP, since brief exchanges need no setup
options.rationale: Correct: short request/response traffic doesn't justify a connection.

options.text: UDP, because it is faster than TCP
options.rationale: Roughly true, but the point is that they need no connection.

options.text: TCP, because they need assured delivery
options.rationale: They use UDP.

options.text: ICMP, because they are control messages
options.rationale: ICMP isn't a transport for applications.

questions.explanation: UDP is connectionless, best-effort delivery: low overhead, no delivery guarantee. Short exchanges like these can retry at the application level instead.
questions.discriminator_tested: UDP: low overhead, no delivery guarantee.

questions.stem: A video-call app runs over UDP, and a few packets are lost during a call. What BEST describes what happens?

options.text: A brief glitch; late audio is useless
options.rationale: Correct: retransmitted audio would arrive too late to play.

options.text: The lost packets aren't recovered
options.rationale: True, but it misses why that is acceptable here.

options.text: TCP retransmits the lost packets automatically
options.rationale: The app uses UDP, which doesn't retransmit.

options.text: The call drops until the connection resets
options.rationale: UDP has no connection to reset.

questions.explanation: TCP is used where accuracy matters; UDP where speed matters more than retransmission, such as voice and video. A brief glitch beats waiting for data that is already out of date.
questions.discriminator_tested: Reliability vs speed trade-off.

questions.stem: A server listens on the ports below. Which two are in the well-known range? (Choose two.)

options.rationale: Correct: within 0-1023.
Correct: within 0-1023.
Registered range (1024-49151).
Registered range.
Dynamic range, typical of client ephemeral ports.

questions.explanation: Port numbers identify the service: well-known 0-1023, registered 1024-49151, dynamic 49152-65535. Servers listen on well-known or registered ports; clients use ephemeral ones.
questions.discriminator_tested: Well-known 0-1023, registered 1024-49151, dynamic 49152-65535.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes the job of IP itself?

options.text: Addressing and routing, with no delivery guarantee
options.rationale: Correct: logical addressing and best-effort routing.

options.text: Moving packets between networks
options.rationale: True, but it leaves out that IP gives no delivery guarantee.

options.text: Ensuring packets arrive in order and complete
options.rationale: That is TCP.

options.text: Mapping IP addresses to MAC addresses
options.rationale: That is ARP.

questions.explanation: IP provides logical addressing and routing of packets. It is connectionless and best-effort and carries no delivery guarantee.
questions.discriminator_tested: IP is connectionless and best-effort.

questions.stem: A firewall team blocks every ICMP message at the perimeter 'for security'. Which side effect is MOST likely?

options.text: Ping and traceroute stop working through it
options.rationale: Correct: they depend on ICMP messages.

options.text: Web browsing stops, since it uses ICMP
options.rationale: Web traffic uses TCP.

options.text: DNS lookups fail, since they use ICMP
options.rationale: DNS uses UDP and TCP.

options.text: ARP stops resolving addresses on the LAN
options.rationale: ARP isn't ICMP and never crosses the perimeter.

questions.explanation: ICMP carries error reporting and diagnostics such as ping and traceroute. It carries control messages, not application data, so blocking it breaks diagnostics rather than applications.
questions.discriminator_tested: ICMP carries control messages, not application data.

questions.stem: A technician runs the commands below on a PC. What does the incomplete entry BEST tell them?
questions.exhibit:
C:\> arp -a
Interface: 10.1.4.20
  Internet Address    Physical Address     Type
  10.1.4.1            00-1a-2b-3c-4d-01    dynamic
  10.1.4.77           (incomplete)
C:\> ping 10.1.4.77
Request timed out.

options.text: No device answered the ARP request
options.rationale: Correct: no MAC was learned for 10.1.4.77.

options.text: 10.1.4.77 is unreachable from this PC
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say what failed: address resolution.

options.text: DNS failed to resolve the host's name
options.rationale: No name was involved; the IP was used directly.

options.text: The router is blocking ARP between subnets
options.rationale: Both addresses are on the same subnet.

questions.explanation: ARP resolves an IPv4 address to a MAC address on the local segment. An incomplete entry means the request went unanswered, so the host is off, disconnected, or not at that address.
questions.discriminator_tested: ARP resolves IPv4 to MAC on the local segment.
